SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 8, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) initiated countervailing duty (CVD) investigations of imports of certain linear hydraulic cylinders and parts thereof (hydraulic cylinders) from China, India, and Mexico.[1]
Currently, the preliminary determinations are due no later than November 12, 2026.
Postponement of Preliminary Determinations
Section 703(b)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), requires Commerce to issue the preliminary determination in a countervailing duty investigation within 65 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation. However, section 703(c)(1) of the Act permits Commerce to postpone the preliminary determination in a CVD investigation until no later than 130 days after the date on which Commerce initiated the investigation if: (A) the petitioner makes a timely request for a postponement; or
( printed page 66295)
(B) Commerce concludes that the parties concerned are cooperating, that the investigation is extraordinarily complicated, and that additional time is necessary to make a preliminary determination. Under 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner must submit a request for postponement 25 days or more before the scheduled date of the preliminary determination and must state the reasons for the request. Commerce will grant the request unless it finds compelling reasons to deny the request.
On October 14, 2026, the petitioner [2]
timely requested that Commerce postpone the preliminary CVD determinations to 130 days from the date of initiation, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.205(b) and (e).[3]
The petitioner stated a postponement is warranted to provide Commerce with additional time to review and analyze questionnaire responses, and issue supplemental questionnaires prior to making preliminary CVD determinations.[4]
In accordance with 19 CFR 351.205(e), the petitioner has stated the reasons for requesting a postponement of the preliminary determinations, and Commerce finds no compelling reason to deny the request. Therefore, in accordance with section 703(c)(1)(A) of the Act, Commerce is postponing the deadline for the preliminary determinations in the CVD investigations of hydraulic cylinders from China, India, and Mexico to no later than 130 days after the date on which these investigations were initiated,
i.e.,
January 19, 2027.[5]
Pursuant to section 705(a)(1) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.210(b)(1), the deadline for the final determinations of these investigations will continue to be 75 days after the date of the preliminary determinations.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published pursuant to section 703(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.205(f)(1).

Toyota Motor Corporation
World's largest automaker by volume
Japan recorded a trade deficit of 536,558 million yen in September 2026 on a provisional basis, according to the country's trade statistics released on October 21, 2026. The figures, published by Japan Customs, show exports rising 16.7 percent year on year to 10,972,254 million yen while imports climbed 18.9 percent to 11,508,812 million yen, leaving the deficit at 93.2 percent of the level recorded a year earlier.
Exports to Asia totaled 6,073,589 million yen, up 17.5 percent, while imports from the region reached 6,026,509 million yen, up 22.2 percent, producing a surplus of 47,080 million yen. Shipments to China fell short of imports, with exports of 1,729,957 million yen against imports of 2,757,246 million yen, a deficit of 1,027,289 million yen.
Exports to the United States rose 22.9 percent to 1,963,025 million yen, while imports from the US increased 44.8 percent to 1,570,216 million yen, leaving a surplus of 392,809 million yen. Exports to the European Union grew 10.5 percent to 985,410 million yen, and imports from the bloc edged down 0.1 percent to 1,126,311 million yen, resulting in a deficit of 140,901 million yen.
Exports to the Middle East declined 12.0 percent to 357,099 million yen, while imports from the region fell 7.0 percent to 815,161 million yen, a deficit of 458,062 million yen. Shipments to Russia dropped 13.4 percent to 30,851 million yen, and imports from Russia rose 24.6 percent to 84,918 million yen.
Transport equipment was the largest export category at 2,284,975 million yen, up 10.8 percent, followed by electrical machinery at 2,147,898 million yen, up 30.3 percent, and machinery at 1,949,789 million yen, up 18.4 percent. Within electrical machinery, semiconductor exports reached 933,673 million yen, an increase of 49.4 percent.
On the import side, mineral fuels were the largest category at 2,346,269 million yen, up 39.4 percent, ahead of electrical machinery at 2,130,340 million yen, up 23.4 percent, and machinery at 1,261,232 million yen, up 27.0 percent. Imports of semiconductors totaled 605,246 million yen, up 5.3 percent.

articles.title: China moves to tighten AI export controls amid US rivalry - Malaysia Sun
articles.summary: China moves to tighten AI export controls amid US rivalry  Malaysia Sun
articles.full_text:
Anabelle Colaco
                
20 Oct 2026, 09:55 GMT+10
            
BEIJING, China: China has proposed export controls on 23 artificial intelligence technologies, including those involving models, agents and computing clusters, as Beijing moves to tighten oversight of technology it considers important to national security and geopolitical competition with Washington.
The proposals would cover overseas deployment of AI models containing restricted technology but exclude access through application programming interfaces, websites, apps and software-as-a-service platforms, China's Commerce Ministry said.
That distinction could allow Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Alibaba to continue expanding internationally while giving Beijing greater oversight of transfers of sensitive AI technology abroad.
Chinese AI models have gained ground overseas because of lower prices and improving capabilities since DeepSeek's R1 model emerged early last year.
Reuters reported in July that Chinese authorities had discussed potentially restricting overseas access to China's most advanced AI models, including unreleased ones, with major technology companies including Alibaba, ByteDance and Z.AI.
The Commerce Ministry said the proposed controls were partly intended to prevent the misuse of AI technologies, including systems capable of autonomously generating and modifying malicious software that could threaten critical infrastructure and national security.
Most AI technologies would remain freely exportable, with simplified licensing for open-source technology exports and Chinese companies operating their own computing centers overseas. Technology already in the public domain through open-source releases or academic papers would also fall outside the proposed controls.
The measures come as China and the United States compete for leadership in AI. Washington's restrictions on China's access to cutting-edge American AI chips needed to train frontier models have helped keep U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI in the lead, although Chinese rivals are finding workarounds to narrow the gap.
At the same time, the two countries have agreed to keep humans in control of nuclear-weapons decisions and last month established a dialogue and incident-communications channel for advanced AI.
The AI proposals form part of a broader revision of China's technology export catalogue covering 40 technologies across AI, biotechnology and solar power.
The proposals also include prohibiting transfers of intellectual property ownership involving some novel cell and gene therapies and small interfering RNA technologies.
Exporters must register certain overseas technology transfers from October 30, pending final rules after public consultation closes on November 15.

articles.title: China tightens drone export controls amid security concerns - Yeni Şafak English
articles.summary: China tightens drone export controls amid security concerns  Yeni Şafak English
articles.full_text:
Beijing announced revised export controls on drones and construction machinery bound for sensitive destinations, citing national security interests with measures effective Nov. 18.
Tightened drone export rules
China's Commerce Ministry announced Monday that revised export controls on drones and critical components will take effect on Nov. 18, requiring government authorization for shipments meeting specified technical thresholds. The rules, issued jointly with customs authorities and the Central Military Commission's Equipment Development Department, target UAV-specific autopilots, certain engines, and unmanned aircraft capable of controlled flight beyond visual range with endurance of at least three hours.
Covered items also include drones with ranges exceeding 300 kilometers, communications equipment, motors, propeller blades, and related software and technologies, according to the ministry. Simplified procedures will apply to qualifying exhibition exports, while eligible companies with effective internal compliance systems may benefit from general licenses.
Machinery restrictions
Beijing also imposed licensing requirements on specialized construction machinery bound for sensitive countries and regions engaged in disputes with China, including tunnel boring machines, certain walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. The controls cover shield and rock tunnel boring machines along with their cutting tools, cutterheads, and main drive systems, while walking excavators are restricted if they exceed specified thresholds for crossing obstacles or wading through water.
Compliance and implementation
Exports to sensitive destinations will require individual licenses, whereas shipments to other markets will use a registration-based export certification procedure, with exporters and end users formally undertaking not to transfer covered Chinese-origin items to sensitive destinations without authorization. The Commerce Ministry said China's dual-use export control list will be updated when the measures enter into force, ensuring alignment with the new regulatory framework.

Japan Posts 2.82 Trillion Yen Trade Deficit for April-September Fiscal 2026
Japan recorded a trade deficit of 2.82 trillion yen for the April to September period of fiscal 2026, according to provisional trade statistics released by Japan Customs. The figures, published by the customs agency on October 21, 2026, show exports rising 18.4 percent year on year to 63.46 trillion yen while imports climbed 20.4 percent to 66.28 trillion yen, widening the shortfall from the same period a year earlier.
Quarterly Breakdown
The April to June quarter produced exports of 30.93 trillion yen, up 17.0 percent, against imports of 31.46 trillion yen, up 15.9 percent, leaving a deficit of 525.0 billion yen. The July to September quarter showed a sharper expansion, with exports of 32.52 trillion yen, up 19.7 percent, and imports of 34.82 trillion yen, up 24.8 percent, for a deficit of 2.29 trillion yen.
Within the six-month period, the January to March quarter had recorded a deficit of 498.0 billion yen, while the October to December 2025 quarter posted a surplus of 157.8 billion yen.
Regional Trade Patterns
Exports to Asia totaled 35.33 trillion yen, up 20.2 percent, and imports from the region reached 33.94 trillion yen, up 26.2 percent, yielding a surplus of 1.39 trillion yen. Trade with China produced a deficit of 4.60 trillion yen as exports rose 17.6 percent to 10.89 trillion yen and imports grew 20.2 percent to 15.50 trillion yen.
Exports to the United States increased 17.2 percent to 11.33 trillion yen, while imports from the United States rose 43.9 percent to 9.21 trillion yen, leaving a surplus of 2.12 trillion yen. Shipments to the European Union grew 17.0 percent to 5.79 trillion yen and imports from the bloc rose 4.2 percent to 6.64 trillion yen, resulting in a deficit of 848.7 billion yen.
Trade with the Middle East showed declines on both sides, with exports down 16.6 percent to 1.70 trillion yen and imports down 18.8 percent to 4.40 trillion yen, producing a deficit of 2.70 trillion yen.
Commodity Detail
Transport equipment was the largest export category at 12.99 trillion yen, up 12.2 percent, including motor vehicles valued at 9.65 trillion yen. Electrical machinery followed at 11.90 trillion yen, up 30.2 percent, with semiconductors accounting for 4.91 trillion yen. Machinery exports totaled 11.03 trillion yen, up 14.6 percent.
On the import side, mineral fuels were the largest category at 12.75 trillion yen, up 24.5 percent, followed by electrical machinery at 11.70 trillion yen, up 17.7 percent, and machinery at 7.37 trillion yen, up 24.4 percent. Chemicals imports reached 7.17 trillion yen, up 18.7 percent, and foodstuffs totaled 5.47 trillion yen, up 4.9 percent.

articles.title: Spain's trade deficit rises 30.5% through August - El Estrecho Digital
articles.summary: Spain's trade deficit rises 30.5% through August  El Estrecho Digital
articles.full_text:
Spain's imports grew between January and August 2026 at twice the pace of exports, and the trade deficit increased 30.5% compared with the same period a year earlier, reaching 45.818 million euros. According to provisional data from DataComex, of the State Secretariat for Trade, compiled by EED Data, El Estrecho Digital's data platform, Spanish sales abroad totaled 264.182 million, up 3.2%. Purchases reached 310.000 million, an increase of 6.5%.
In absolute terms, imports increased by 18.974 million and exports by 8.261 million. The difference translates into 10.713 million more in deficit than in the first eight months of 2025, when the negative balance was 35.106 million, according to the monthly series compiled by EED Data. The coverage ratio, which measures what share of purchases is paid for by sales, falls to 85.2%, compared with 87.9% a year earlier. In other words, Spain sells 85 euros abroad for every 100 it buys from abroad, almost three euros less than a year ago.
The deterioration is concentrated in the last five months. At the end of March, the cumulative deficit was lower than a year earlier: 11.677 million, compared with 15.100 million in the first quarter of 2025. Between April and August, by contrast, the negative balance totaled 34.141 million, 14.135 million more than in the same months of the previous year.
August, the latest month available, saw higher growth rates in both flows. Spanish exports totaled 27.595 million, 13.3% more than in August 2025, while imports reached 35.408 million, up 16.7%. The monthly deficit was 7.813 million, compared with 5.983 million a year earlier, and coverage fell to 77.9%. The comparison starts from a low base, as August 2025 was the month with the lowest export value in the last 24 months of the series, at 24.351 million. The negative balance in August 2026 is the second largest in that period, exceeded only by May of this year, at 8.245 million.
Energy explains a significant portion of the figures, although not most of the deterioration. Chapter 27 of the tariff, which groups mineral fuels, mineral oils and products of their distillation, ranks first in imports, at 43.129 million, up 16.9%. It leaves a negative balance of 25.414 million, 55.5% of the total deficit. It also ranks third in exports, at 17.714 million after growing 29.3%. Those additional 4.017 million account for almost half (48.6%) of the increase in Spanish sales abroad during the period. Without Chapter 27, exports would have grown 1.8%.
However, the worsening balance is mainly due to the rest of trade. The energy deficit increased by 2.211 million compared with January–August 2025. By contrast, the balance excluding Chapter 27 went from a negative balance of 11.902 million to one of 20.404 million, an increase of 8.502 million. Excluding energy, imports grow 5% and exports 1.8%, while coverage stands at 92.4%.
The chapter for motor vehicles, tractors and other land vehicles, which ranks first in exports, accounts for much of this change. Sales totaled 35.459 million, up 0.8%, but purchases grew 14.1%, reaching 35.286 million. The chapter's surplus, which was 4.238 million in the first eight months of 2025, has fallen to 173 million. This decline of 4.065 million is equivalent to 37.9% of the increase in Spain's trade deficit during the period.
In the following industrial chapters, purchases also grow more than sales. Exports of machinery and mechanical appliances total 19.126 million, up 4.7%, against imports of 29.927 million, up 7%. In electrical machinery and equipment, sales reach 15.018 million (+7%) and purchases 28.419 million (+10.7%). Pharmaceutical products show the opposite trend. Both exports, down 11% to 12.342 million, and imports, down 13% to 15.264 million, fall, and the negative balance shrinks from 3.669 to 2.922 million. Among agri-food chapters, fruit totals 8.701 million (+2.7%), vegetables 6.728 million (+6.5%) and meat 6.163 million, down 13.1%.
By country, China is Spain's leading supplier, at 35.879 million, up 11.1% and accounting for 11.6% of all imports. Spanish exports to China, by contrast, remain virtually stable at 5.383 million (+0.7%), or 2% of the total. The bilateral balance is negative by 30.496 million, with coverage at 15%, a figure equivalent to two-thirds of Spain's trade deficit. Germany, at 33.687 million (+2.5%), and France, at 26.222 million (+7%), follow as suppliers. Purchases from the United Kingdom rise 14.9% to 8.365 million, while those from the United States remain stable at 20.753 million.
France is the leading destination for Spanish sales, at 38.014 million, 14.4% of the total and up 3.6%. Germany follows at 27.115 million (+4.7%), Portugal at 24.161 million (+9.8%), and Italy at 22.750 million (+10.7%). Outside the European Union, the United Kingdom buys 17.629 million from Spain (+2.8%), the United States 11.944 million (+6%) and Morocco, the eighth-largest destination, 8.343 million (+2.9%). Exports to the Netherlands fall 14.3% to 8.739 million, and to Belgium 10% to 7.709 million.
By province, Barcelona totals 52.580 million in sales abroad (+2%) and Madrid 35.717 million (+0.6%). Valencia reaches 14.745 million, up 7.4%, and Bizkaia records the largest increase among the top ten, up 15% to 8.093 million. Pontevedra, fourth with 9.841 million, declines 4.4%. Andalusia, with 28.617 million, increases its exports by 5.8% and accounts for 10.8% of the national total.
Over the last twelve months, from September 2025 to August 2026, Spanish exports totaled 395.353 million (+2.6%) and imports 463.120 million (+6%). The deficit accumulated over that period, 67.767 million, exceeds that for all of 2025, which was 57.055 million. The August figures extend the trend already evident in the cumulative total through July. The figures are provisional until finalized by Customs. DataComex publishes monthly data with a lag of about two months, so the September cumulative total is expected to be released in November. The complete series by products and countries can be consulted in the Foreign Trade section of EED Data.

articles.title: Catalonia shoots up the trade deficit with China - Diari ARA
articles.summary: Catalonia shoots up the trade deficit with China  Diari ARA
articles.full_text:
After the pandemic, the negative balance with the Asian country regularly exceeds €1,000M monthly
BarcelonaCatalonia's trade deficit with China reached 12.37 billion euros last year, a result that doubles the negative trade balance recorded in 2015 and is 236% larger than that of 2005, according to data from the Spanish government. In recent years, the monthly trade deficit with China has in many cases exceeded 1 billion euros, levels that double the negative balances from before the pandemic. The sector where Chinese imports are growing the most is finished automobiles and motorcycles: during 2025 it reached 1.557 billion euros in imports, fourteen times more than the 96.7 million in 2019, and far exceeds the 6.41 million exported last year from Catalonia to Beijing in this area.
In August of this year, the last month with data, Catalonia's trade deficit with China was 1.0494 billion euros, according to figures updated this Tuesday by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Enterprise and collected by the ACN. Specifically, Catalonia sold 126.4 million euros to the Asian giant, while it imported 1.1757 billion. The deficit result is the second highest for an eighth month of the year in the historical series, only behind August 2022, when Catalonia's trade balance with China was a negative 1.1909 billion euros.
If the calculation between January and August is analyzed, Catalonia's trade deficit with China rises to 7.77224 billion euros, a figure that remains 89% above the 4.1117 billion for the same period in 2016 and 182% above the 2.75742 billion recorded between January and August 2006, two decades ago.
The most significant year in the escalation of Catalonia's trade deficit with China was 2022. Before that date, a negative trade balance of 8 billion euros accumulated in twelve months had never been exceeded, while that year the result climbed to 13.138 billion euros after growing 68% compared to 2021.
China is the country with which Catalonia has the largest trade deficit. Last year, the balance was a negative 12.37 billion euros, almost double that of the second country, Germany, with 6.333 billion euros. The third country is the Netherlands, with 3.035 billion euros.
However, Catalonia also has notable trade surpluses with other countries that compensate, in part, for the deficits. The surplus ranking was led last year by France, with 6.406 billion euros; Portugal, with 4.543 billion, and the United Kingdom, with 3.832 billion.
The sectors that imported the most from China last year were capital goods (4.238 billion), consumer manufactures (4.154 billion), semi-manufactures (2.596 billion), and the automotive sector as a whole (1.815 billion). Imports from all sectors totaled nearly 14.449 billion euros, which are partially offset by exports.
In the case of finished automobiles and motorcycles, which is the area where imports have climbed the most in recent years, Catalonia bought 1.557 billion of these products from China, fourteen times more than in 2019, the last fiscal year before the outbreak of the pandemic. Between January and August 2026, the sector accumulated 1.1124 billion euros in imports of these products from the Asian country, 11.7% more compared to the 995.6 million in the same period last year.
Increase in exports and imports
Apart from the trade relationship with China, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Business published its monthly foreign trade report for Spain for August this Tuesday. According to the document, exports of Catalan goods reached 6,769.9 million euros in August, 5% above the 6,448 million of the same month last year, the highest figure for an August since 2023 and the third highest in the historical series for the eighth month of the year. At the same time, imports also rose by 4.8% year-on-year, to 8,333 million euros, the highest figure ever seen in an August. The comparison between exports and imports results in a trade deficit of 1,563.1 million euros in August in Catalonia, 3.8% more than last year.
In the annual tally between January and August, Catalonia has accumulated 68,098.4 million euros in exports, 2% more than in the same period last year, and 78,490.4 million in imports, 2.6% more. In total, Catalonia's trade deficit with foreign countries rises to 10,392 million euros between January and August, 6.7% more than a year ago.
Since 2021, Catalonia – like Spain as a whole – has strung together years with economic growth rates higher than the European Union average, driven by consumption by families and foreign tourists, but also by business and administration investment (thanks above all to the Next Generation funds). In contexts of growth driven by activity within the territory, it is common for the trade deficit with foreign countries to increase, as domestic production is insufficient to cover demand and companies turn to foreign suppliers.

articles.title: The EU is facing difficulties in resolving its trade deficit with China. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: The EU is facing difficulties in resolving its trade deficit with China.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The European Union (EU) is considering granting the European Commission (EC) more import-limiting powers to reduce its trade deficit with China, but the proposal faces internal consensus and legal hurdles.
According to international media, at the summit that concluded on October 16 in Brussels, leaders of the 27 EU countries urged the European Commission to urgently develop a new set of trade defense tools. This included a proposal for an "emergency brake" mechanism, allowing the agency to quickly impose quotas or tariffs on imports.
The leaders also approved the trade agreement reached in Beijing earlier in October, under which China voluntarily agreed to reduce its electric vehicle exports to Europe by nearly half. However, member states argued that this concession was insufficient to resolve larger issues in bilateral trade relations.
The EU is facing a trade deficit of over 360 billion euros with China in 2026, equivalent to approximately 1 billion euros per day. EC President Ursula von der Leyen has repeatedly warned Beijing that this situation cannot continue.
Nevertheless, the latest EU figures show that Chinese exports to the bloc continued to increase by 25% in the first eight months of 2026. Pressure has spread from the automotive sector to chemicals and industrial machinery, sectors that are increasingly vulnerable to the influx of Chinese exports.
A decade ago, the EU had an annual deficit of €71 billion in industrial machinery trade with China, but still had a surplus of €6 billion in chemicals. Now, the machinery deficit has increased to €206 billion, while the chemical sector has shifted to a trade deficit of €24 billion annually.
At the conference, Belgium, Denmark, France, and Germany supported the EC's swift action to protect these sectors. Anti-dumping investigations into chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and machinery are expected to be launched in the coming weeks. Wind turbines manufactured in China may also soon be subject to investigation.
You may also like
The proposal to expand the EC's powers was outlined in a joint letter dated October 5th by French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The two leaders argued that the EC should have the power to block goods from accessing the European single market when a trading partner deliberately ignores requests to restore fair competition conditions.
This tool could be used when imports of a particular product group surge unexpectedly and the partner has no way to address it. The proposal also takes into account the possibility of a country using pressure, such as cutting off the supply of essential raw materials, to avoid substantive negotiations on trade imbalances. A German government official explained that the EU needs to be able to inflict damage commensurate with the losses the bloc suffers.
The new proposal could significantly expand the EC's authority in the field of trade. Currently, before applying safeguard measures, the agency must conduct an investigation, provide evidence of unfair competition, and obtain the approval of a majority of member states.
If approved, the new mechanism would allow the EC to streamline investigation procedures and proactively impose tariffs or block imports on a group of goods, without waiting for member states' approval.
This adjustment could limit Beijing's response options, such as launching investigations into European goods or using economic incentives to lobby individual EU member states to oppose the EC's measure.
Analysts suggest that concerns about the possibility of the EC being granted more powers were the main reason China accepted the rare concession on electric vehicle exports. Beijing may have hoped the deal would help close the debate over tougher trade measures. However, that concession reinforced EU countries' belief that the proposed “emergency brake” had caused China to back down, potentially prompting the bloc to continue exerting pressure.
However, the determination to act does not equate to a consensus on how to implement it. The major EU economies support the proposal, but many governments may be hesitant to grant the EC the power to make crucial trade decisions without prior consultation or approval.
You may also like
The scope of application is also a sensitive issue. EU officials avoid specifying which countries the mechanism targets, because a regulation aimed solely at China would be difficult to legally defend at the World Trade Organization (WTO). Such a regulation could also embarrass European countries wishing to maintain friendly relations with Beijing.
Currently, the proposal lacks legal documentation, activation conditions, and agreed-upon scope. The EC expects to submit the plan before the end of 2026, but even if approved, observers in Brussels believe the new powers may not be implemented until the second half of 2027.
Meanwhile, political pressure in Europe continues to mount. On October 7th, the European Parliament adopted a resolution designating China's industrial policy as an existential threat to the EU, with 454 votes in favor, 86 against, and 110 abstentions.

AGENCY:
Office of Electricity, Department of Energy.
ACTION:
Notice of application.
SUMMARY:
Clear Power LLC (the Applicant or Clear Power) has applied for authorization to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico pursuant to the Federal Power Act.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before November 19, 2026.
The United States Department of Energy (DOE) regulates electricity exports from the United States to foreign countries in accordance with section 202(e) of the Federal Power Act (FPA) (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)) and regulations thereunder (10 CFR 205.300). Sections 301(b) and 402(f) of the DOE Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7151(b) and 7172(f)) transferred this regulatory authority, previously exercised by the now-defunct Federal Power Commission, to DOE.
Section 202(e) of the FPA provides that an entity which seeks to export electricity must obtain an order from DOE authorizing that export (16 U.S.C. 824a(e)). On January 8, 2026, the authority to issue such orders was delegated to the DOE's Assistant Secretary for the Office of Electricity by Redelegation Order No. S3-DEL-OE1-2026.
On April 16, 2026, Clear Power filed an application (Application or App.) with DOE for renewal of export authority to transmit electric energy from the United States to Mexico for an additional five-year term. App. at 1. Clear Power was originally granted export authorization under Order No. EA-487 on December 9, 2020, which expired on December 9, 2025. Since Clear Power did not apply for renewal until after the expiration of the current export authorization, DOE is processing the application as a request for a new export authorization.
According to the Application, Clear Power is a limited liability corporation with its principal place of business in Folsom, California. The Applicant is a power marketer with “authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to market electric energy and capacity at wholesale pursuant to market-based rate authorization.”
Id.
at 2. Clear Power states that it is a “wholly-owned subsidiary of the Alaywan Trust, which owns or is affiliated with entities that own or control a combined total of 18.0 MW (nameplate) of operating renewable generation facilities all located in the California Independent System Operator (CAISO) market.”
Id.
Clear Power “does not own or control any electric power generation, transmission distribution facilities” and “does not have a franchised service area”
Id.
at 3. Thus, the Applicant states that it has “no `transmission system' of its own on which power exports could have a reliability or stability impact.”
Id.
at 5. Clear Power “will schedule its exports from the U.S. in compliance with all applicable reliability criteria, standards and guides as are set out by the North American Electricity Reliability Corporation (NERC) (or any successor organization), the North American Energy Standards Board (or any successor organization) and regional reliability councils and as applied by U.S. transmission providers.”
Id.
at 5-6.
The existing international transmission facilities to be utilized by the Applicant have been previously authorized by Presidential permits issued pursuant to Executive Order 10485, as amended, and are appropriate for open access transmission by third parties.
See
App. at Exhibit C.

articles.title: United Airlines CEO faces rightwing backlash after calling for US wealth tax
articles.summary: Scott Kirby says wealth inequality is a ‘danger to society’ and calls for inheritance tax in recent interviewScott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust. articles.full_text:
Scott Kirby, the CEO of United Airlines, is under scrutiny from conservative politicians and commentators for saying wealth inequality is a “danger to society” and calling for a national wealth and inheritance tax in a recent interview.
Talking to the New York Times, Kirby was asked about the growing public distrust of CEOs and whether he felt any responsibility to quell that distrust.
“We should have a national wealth tax – it won’t work by state because people will just move,” he said. “And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them.”
In response, headlines from Fox Business and the New York Post decried that Kirby made $32m in 2025. In response to Kirby’s comments, Glenn Beck, a former Fox News host, and other users on X called for a boycott of United Airlines. Jeff Landry, Louisiana’s governor, said the statement was “audacious”.
“How audacious from a guy that didn’t even build @united and makes $32 million a year,” he wrote on X, adding a link to a government website to donate money to the government. “Better yet, he should distribute his salary to the employees at the bottom of the ladder @united!”
“Let’s see you step up and place your money where your mouth is!” Landry added.
The comment comes just two weeks before voters in California will decide on a so-called “billionaire’s tax”, which would put a 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, that the wealthy have been spending millions fighting against.
Kirby was also asked about the rising cost of flying and said that high prices this year were being compared to the “artificial low” prices from the pandemic, which largely halted travel and highly disrupted the airline industry.
“We have to charge enough that it covers the cost of flying, and it’s expensive to fly airplanes,” he said.
When asked about the $70 passengers must pay to sit in an aisle or window seat if they aren’t a frequent flyer with United, Kirby responded that “the way to give everyone what they want is to charge for the services and products that those customers want,” adding: “There are customers that pay more that get more.”
Kirby also maintained that fares were still lower than in 2019 after adjusting for inflation. According to data from the labor department, the index for airline fares increased by about 20% from September 2019 to September 2026, while overall consumer prices increased by 31%.

articles.full_text:
A judge dismissed a lawsuit filed by Sam Altman’s sister against him on Tuesday. Ann Altman accused the OpenAI CEO of repeatedly sexually abusing her more than two decades ago, which he has denied.
In dismissing Ann Altman’s lawsuit, the US district judge Zachary Bluestone wrote that she had refused to appear for an independent medical examination despite warnings that failure to do so would result in the case’s dismissal.
Laura Politi, a lawyer for Ann Altman, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Santos Perez, a lawyer who previously represented Ann Altman in the case but withdrew this month, said in a statement: “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”
Ann Altman brought her lawsuit in St Louis, Missouri, federal court in January 2025.
Lawyers for Sam Altman did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Ann Altman accused her brother of sexually abusing and raping her between 1997 and 2006 at their family home in suburban Clayton, Missouri, starting when she was three and he was 12. She said the last acts of sexual abuse and rape occurred when Sam Altman was an adult. He is now 41.
The Altman family has said Ann Altman has mental health challenges and received financial support. Sam Altman has said she began accusing him on social media of sexual abuse after the family rejected her demands for more funds.

articles.title: European air fares could rise by as much as 20% in 2027, Ryanair boss predicts
articles.summary: Conflict in Middle East is pushing jet fuel costs higher and many carriers are not hedged against such increases, Michael O’Leary saysRyanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in th...
articles.full_text:
Ryanair’s chief executive has predicted a record increase in European air fares next year, as airlines grapple with fuel bills pushed higher by the Middle East conflict.
Many carriers are not hedged against rising jet fuel costs, Michael O’Leary said, which he predicted would lead to airline bankruptcies and takeovers. He forecast these pressures would result in the price of plane tickets rising by as much as 20%.
“You’re going to see air fares rise next year in Europe, I think by 10, 15, maybe 20%. You’re going to see the biggest increase in air fares, I would say, in history in Europe for the next 12 months,” O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels.
Jet fuel prices have soared in recent months, as the war on Iran has choked off fuel supplies. Jet fuel accounts for a large portion of carriers’ costs. The airlines body IATA previously predicted jet fuel prices would be 70% higher across 2026 – estimated to average $152 (£114) a barrel for the year, compared with $90 in 2025 – slashing airlines’ profits.
Ryanair and many other European airlines had hedged their jet fuel requirements for 2026, O’Leary said, adding that Ryanair was 80% hedged at $67 a barrel at the time the Iran conflict began in late February.
However, the boss of Europe’s largest airline said most European carriers, including Ryanair, do not have significant hedging in place from April 2027 onwards to protect them if oil prices remain high.
“We’re 85% unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” O’Leary said.
Ryanair’s hedging contract for 2027 covered 15% of its fuel costs at $85 a barrel, he added, whereas spot rates are currently hovering at about double that level.
EasyJet reported a £105m annual rise in fuel costs in July, adding it had hedged 62% of its fuel requirements for the first half of 2027 and 37% for the second half of the year. The airline announced in October it was cutting 700,000 seats from its winter schedule in an attempt to save fuel.
During his visit to Brussels, O’Leary announced he was cutting 20 of Ryanair’s routes and more than one million seats from Belgium from the airline’s winter schedule, after the federal government’s decision to increase its aviation tax from €2 to €7 in January.
O’Leary is the latest executive to warn of the downbeat outlook for aviation. Industry leaders have said some carriers will struggle to survive the fuel price shock. Passenger surveys have shown travellers are braced for higher fares and are prepared to spend more, but airlines do not know how long consumers will be able to afford pricier tickets.

articles.full_text:
India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

AGENCY:
Department of the Navy, Department of Defense.
ACTION:
Notice of Issuance of Certificate of Alternate Compliance.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Navy hereby announces that a Certificate of Alternate Compliance has been issued for USS PATRICK GALLAGHER (DDG 127). Due to the special construction and purpose of this vessel, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy has determined it is a vessel of the Navy which, due to its special construction and purpose, cannot comply fully with the navigation lights provisions of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS) without interfering with its special function as a naval ship. The intended effect of this notice is to warn mariners in waters where 72 COLREGS apply.
DATES:
This Certificate of Alternate Compliance is effective October 20, 2026 and is applicable beginning April 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Lieutenant Commander Jordan Foley, JAGC, U.S. Navy, Admiralty Attorney, Office of the Judge Advocate General, Admiralty and Claims Division (Code 15A), 1322 Patterson Ave. SE, Suite 3000, Washington Navy Yard, DC 20374-5066, 202-685-5040, or
admiralty@us.navy.mil.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background and Purpose. Executive Order (E.O.) 11964 (42 FR 4327; January 19, 1977) and 33 U.S.C. 1605 provide that the requirements of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS), as to the number, position, range, or arc of visibility of lights or shapes, as well as to the disposition and characteristics of sound-signaling appliances, shall not
( printed page 66320)
apply to a vessel or class of vessels of the Navy where the Secretary of the Navy shall find and certify that, by reason of special construction or purpose, it is not possible for such vessel(s) to comply fully with the provisions without interfering with the special function of the vessel(s). Notice of issuance of a Certificate of Alternate Compliance must be made in the
Federal Register
.
In accordance with 33 U.S.C. 1605, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy, under authority delegated by the Secretary of the Navy, hereby finds and certifies that USS PATRICK GALLAGHER (DDG 127) is a vessel of special construction or purpose, and that, with respect to the position of the following navigational lights, it is not possible to comply fully with the requirements of the provisions enumerated in the 72 COLREGS without interfering with the special function of the vessel: Annex I, paragraph 3(a), pertaining to the position of the forward masthead light; Annex I, paragraph 2(f)(i) pertaining to the vertical position of the aft masthead light; Annex I, paragraph 3(a), pertaining to the horizontal distance between the masthead lights; Annex I, paragraph 3(c), pertaining to the horizontal distance of the “task lights” below the masthead lights; Annex I, paragraph 2(f)(ii), pertaining to the horizontal position of the task lights above the aft masthead light(s) and vertical position of the task lights between the forward masthead light(s) and aft masthead light(s).
The Admiralty Counsel of the Navy further finds and certifies that these navigational lights are in closest possible compliance with the applicable provision of the 72 COLREGS.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Title of Collection:
Grantee Reporting Requirements for the U.S. National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines (NSF Engines) Program.

3145-0284.
Expiration Date of Approval:
December 31, 2026.
Type of Request:
Request for approval to renew an information collection.
Proposed Project:
The U.S. National Science Foundation Regional Innovation Engines (Engines) program, led by NSF's Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships (TIP), is NSF's flagship investment in place-based innovation. Established pursuant to the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, the program invests in regions across the United States to bring together the research, talent, partnerships, and resources needed to turn advances in science and technology into economic and societal benefits. Each NSF Engine serves a defined geographic Region of Service (RoS), the area intended to benefit from the NSF Engine's activities and investments, and is organized around technologies and challenges important to that region and the Nation.
Specifically, the program seeks to:
Advance key technology areas critical to U.S. competitiveness;
Address pressing national and societal challenges;
Cultivate partnerships across industry, academia, government, nonprofit organizations, civil society and communities of practice;
Promote economic growth and job creation; and
Develop the regional workforce and talent needed to sustain innovation.
Each NSF Engine carries out these objectives through three core functions: use-inspired research and development, translation of innovation results to society, and workforce development. Together, these activities are intended to strengthen a RoS's capacity to develop and commercialize new technologies, create and grow businesses, prepare workers for new opportunities, and attract additional investment. Over time, NSF Engines are expected to develop into sustainable regional innovation ecosystems that contribute to economic growth and U.S. competitiveness.
NSF Engines are substantial, long-term investments. Each NSF Engine may receive NSF funding for up to 10 years, based on its performance and progress toward established goals and milestones. As NSF Engines develop, their activities, partnerships, and sources of support are expected to grow and evolve. Regular reporting on a defined cadence helps NSF Engines teams track performance, identify and address issues, and adjust their strategies as needed. At the same time, it allows NSF to assess progress across the portfolio, identify risks and emerging challenges, and make informed program management and funding decisions.
Project Reporting Requirements:
NSF is seeking renewed approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for the revised
Grantee Reporting Requirements for NSF Engines Program
information collection. The collection consists of four reporting components: (1) Quarterly Reports; (2) the Engine Report Template; (3) the Strategic and Implementation Plan; and (4) the Strategic Growth Plan. Each serves a distinct purpose; together, they provide NSF with information to monitor the implementation, performance, and development of each NSF Engine over the life of the award and the program holistically.
Quarterly Reports
will be required in the first quarter (Q1) and third quarter (Q3) of the first year. These reports provide timely information on NSF Engine operations, implementation, performance, and emerging issues. The two
Quarterly Reports

AGENCY:
Department of the Navy, Department of Defense.
                    ACTION:
Notice of Issuance of Certificate of Alternate Compliance.
                    SUMMARY:
The U.S. Navy hereby announces that a Certificate of Alternate Compliance has been issued for USS HARRISBURG (LPD 30). Due to the special construction and purpose of this vessel, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy has determined it is a vessel of the Navy which, due to its special construction and purpose, cannot comply fully with the navigation lights provisions of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS) without interfering with its special function as a naval ship. The intended effect of this notice is to warn mariners in waters where 72 COLREGS apply.
                    DATES:
This Certificate of Alternate Compliance is effective October 20, 2026 and is applicable beginning August 20, 2026.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
                    Background and Purpose.
                     Executive Order (E.O.) 11964 (42 FR 4327; January 19, 1977) and 33 U.S.C. 1605 provide that the requirements of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (72 COLREGS), as to the number, position, range, or arc of visibility of lights or shapes, as well as to the disposition and characteristics of sound-signaling appliances, shall not apply to a vessel or class of vessels of the Navy where the Secretary of the Navy shall find and certify that, by reason of special construction or purpose, it is not possible for such vessel(s) to comply fully with the provisions without interfering with the special function of the vessel(s). Notice of issuance of a Certificate of Alternate Compliance must be made in the 
                    Federal Register
                    .
                
In accordance with 33 U.S.C. 1605, the Admiralty Counsel of the Navy, under authority delegated by the Secretary of the Navy, hereby finds and certifies that USS HARRISBURG (LPD 30) is a vessel of special construction or purpose, and that, with respect to the position of the following navigational lights, it is not possible to comply fully with the requirements of the provisions enumerated in the 72 COLREGS without interfering with the special function of the vessel: Annex I, Paragraph 2(i)(i) pertaining to the vertical position of the task lights in relation to one another; Annex I, Paragraph 3(a), pertaining to the horizontal separation of the masthead lights; Annex I, Paragraph 2 (k), pertaining to the vertical separation of the anchor lights.
The Admiralty Counsel of the Navy further finds and certifies that these navigational lights are in closest possible compliance with the applicable provision of the 72 COLREGS.
(Authority: 33 U.S.C. 1605(c), E.O. 11964.)
                    M.A. Tabach,
Lieutenant Commander, Judge Advocate General's Corps, U.S. Navy, Federal Register Liaison Officer.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This notice informs the public that HUD is seeking approval from OMB for the information collection described in Section A.
A. Overview of Information Collection
Title of Information Collection:
Data Collection for HUD's Innovative Housing Showcase
OMB Approval Number:
2528-0346.
Type of Request:
Revision.
Form Number:
N/A.
Description of the need for the information and proposed use:
The Innovative Housing Showcase (IHS) is a public event to raise awareness of new, innovative housing technologies, especially offsite constructed or factory-built housing. HUD is seeking potential exhibitors who have developed innovative housing technologies to show their technologies to the public.
HUD seeks to collect information to identify exhibitors for the Innovative Housing Showcase (Showcase) and obtain information from exhibitors after the Showcase. Exhibitors provide key information about their products, allowing HUD to review and make informed decisions on this innovation to accept. The application form streamlines information collection by focusing on information required to vet the specific product that will be exhibited. The changes are a revision per the addition of a post-exhibit questionnaire. This new questionnaire solicits information from exhibitors on how to improve future showcases and how HUD can make the event more valuable for their company. It will not collect sensitive or proprietary information.
Respondents:
Product manufacturers, innovators, and construction industry stakeholders.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
100.
Estimated Number of Responses:
160 (100 applicants and 60 responses are exhibitors who complete the exit interview after the end of the Showcase).
Frequency of Response:
2.
Average Hours per Response:
3 hours for application and .5 hours for the exit interview.
Total Estimated Burdens:
The cost to respondents to complete an application is estimated at the marketing manager's median hourly wage rate ($79.70) for 3 hours of work. The total estimated cost is $26,301 ($23,910 + $2,391).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under part 211 of title 49 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), this document provides the public notice that by letter dated April 27, 2026, MACZ petitioned FRA for an extension of a special approval of an alternate standard for periodic brake equipment maintenance per 49 CFR parts 229 (Railroad Locomotive Safety Standards) and 238 (Passenger Equipment Safety Standards). The relevant Docket Number is FRA-2008-0065.
Specifically, MACZ requests approval to continue applying alternate standards for the CCB-KE-3.9 air brake system of the MARC HHP-8 locomotive fleet. This alternate standard to 49 CFR 229.29(e),
Air brake system calibration, maintenance, and testing,
and 238.309(a)(2),
Periodic brake equipment maintenance—General,
allows for an increase in the level two and level three maintenance intervals to 2,944 days (8 years). MACZ explains that it continues
( printed page 66388)
to maintain the air brake systems in accordance with the existing conditions of relief in this docket, and that it has realized a high level of reliability with the air brake system. Further, MACZ indicates that the locomotives are expected to continue in passenger service for MACZ, operated and maintained by Amtrak on the Northeast Corridor, for the foreseeable future.
A copy of the petition, as well as any written communications concerning the petition, is available for review online at
www.regulations.gov.
Interested parties are invited to participate in these proceedings by submitting written views, data, or comments. FRA does not anticipate scheduling a public hearing in connection with these proceedings since the facts do not appear to warrant a hearing. If any interested party desires an opportunity for oral comment and a public hearing, they should notify FRA, in writing, before the end of the comment period and specify the basis for their request.
Communications received by December 21, 2026 will be considered by FRA before final action is taken. Comments received after that date will be considered if practicable.

as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14 FDMS), which can be reviewed at
https://www.transportation.gov/privacy.
See also
https://www.regulations.gov/privacy-notice
for the privacy notice of
regulations.gov.
Issued in Washington, DC.
John Karl Alexy,
Associate Administrator for Railroad Safety, Chief Safety Officer.

ACTION:
Notice of order.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Homeland Security is publishing notice of the Secretary of Homeland Security's issuance of an order (1) excluding information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in applicable regulations, from federal civilian agency procurements; and, (2) removing all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology.
Pursuant to the authority granted by the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, 41 U.S.C. 1321-1328, and implementing regulations at 41 CFR 201-1, following review of the Federal Acquisition Security Council Recommendation and affiliated evidence, the Secretary of Homeland Security has ordered: (1) exclusion of information technology products and services developed by Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd (DeepSeek), to include affiliated entities as defined in 48 CFR 2.101, from federal civilian agency procurements; and (2) removal of all DeepSeek and DeepSeek-affiliate products, and third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations, from civilian agency information technology.
A copy of the signed order is contained in the accompanying Appendix and can be found at

by searching for DHS Docket Number DHS-2026-0628.

Title:
Federal Credit Union Occupancy, Planning, and Disposal of Acquired and Abandoned Premises—12 CFR 701.36.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
Section 107(4) of the Federal Credit Union Act authorizes a federal credit union (FCU) to purchase, hold, and dispose of property necessary or incidental to its operations. Section 701.36 of NCUA Rules and Regulations interprets and implements this provision of the FCU Act by establishing occupancy, planning, and disposal requirements for acquired and abandoned premises. It also prohibits certain transactions. In addition, this section includes provisions in which an FCU may seek a waiver from certain requirements of the rule. NCUA reviews written waiver requests and makes a determination on the request based on safety and soundness considerations.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
Part 725 contains the regulations implementing the National Credit Union Central Liquidity Facility Act, subchapter III of the Federal Credit Union Act. The NCUA Central Liquidity Facility is a mixed-ownership Government corporation within NCUA. It is managed by the NCUA Board and is owned by its member credit unions. The purpose of the Facility is to improve the general financial stability of credit unions by meeting their liquidity needs and thereby encourage savings, support consumer and mortgage lending and provide basic financial resources to all segments of the economy. The Central Liquidity Facility achieves this purpose through operation of a Central Liquidity Fund (CLF). The collection of information under this part is necessary for the CLF to determine credit worthiness, as required by 12 U.S.C. 1795e(2).
Title:
Organization and Operations of Federal Credit Unions—Loan Participation, 12 CFR 701.22.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
NCUA Rules and Regulations, sections 701.22 and 741.225, outline the requirements for a loan participation program. FICUs are required to execute a written loan participation agreement with the lead lender. Additionally, the rule requires all FICUs to maintain a loan participation policy that establishes underwriting standards and maximum concentration limits. Credit unions may apply for waivers on certain key provisions of the rule.
Title:
Capital Planning and Stress Testing, 12 CFR 702-E.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
To protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) and the credit union system, the largest Federally Insured Credit Unions (FICUs) must have systems and processes to monitor and maintain their capital adequacy. The rule requires covered credit unions to develop and maintain a capital plan and submit this plan to NCUA by March 31 of each year. The rule applies to all FICUs that report $10 billion or more in assets on their March 31 Call Report.
Type of Review:
Extension of a previously approved collection.
Abstract:
The NCUA Board (Board) has determined, to protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF) and the credit union system, that the largest Federally Insured Credit Unions (FICUs) should have systems and processes in place to monitor and maintain their capital adequacy.
Subpart C of part 702 of NCUA's regulations codifies capital planning and stress testing requirements for federally insured credit unions with $10 billion or more in assets (covered credit unions).
Covered credit unions are further delineated by asset tiers.
Tier I are credit union with $10 billion or more in total assets, but less than $15 billion in total assets; tier II are credit union with $15 billion or more in total assets, but less than $20 billion in total assets; and tier III are credit union with $20 billion or more in total assets.
Tier II and III credit unions are required to conduct supervisory stress tests and section 702.
306 (b) codifies that NCUA reserves the right to conduct stress tests of covered credit unions at any time and where both NCUA and a covered credit union have conducted the tests, the results of NCUA's tests will determine whether the covered credit union has met the requirements of this subpart.
To facilitate NCUA's ability to conduct supervisory stress test on covered credit unions, section 702.
306(d) requires that covered credit unions must provide NCUA with any relevant qualitative or quantitative information requested by NCUA pertinent to capital plans or stress test under this part.

Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for Office of Management and Budget approval. All comments will become a matter of public record. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission) has prepared a draft policy statement concerning the Commission's review of operational air emissions and associated air quality effects of proposed natural gas projects under the Natural Gas Act (NGA) and the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). Pursuant to the policy described in the draft statement, the Commission would no longer ordinarily ask applicants to prepare or submit air dispersion modeling for compressor stations or liquefied natural gas facilities, nor require use of the results of such modeling in assessing the air quality effects of such facilities under the NGA and NEPA. Double E states that the Project will also strengthen the reliability and operational flexibility of the Double E system across Texas and New Mexico and give the system the capability to reverse the direction of flow on its mainline. Double E estimates the total cost of the Project to be $103,839,697 and proposes to use its existing recourse rates under Rate Schedule FTS as the applicable recourse rates for firm transportation service to be provided by the Project, all as more fully set forth in the application which is on file with the Commission and open for public inspection.

On October 1, 2026, and supplemented on October 13, 2026, Zushi Renewables, LLC, filed a notice of intent to construct a qualifying conduit hydropower facility, pursuant to section 30 of the Federal Power Act (FPA). The proposed Arvin Edison Canal Hydrokinetic 1 Project would have an installed capacity of 40 kilowatts (kW) and would be located along the Arvin-Edison Water Storage District's Intake Canal, near Bakersfield, Kern County, California.
Qualifying Conduit Hydropower Facility Description:
The project would consist of: (1) four 10-kW modular hydrokinetic twin turbines, for a total capacity of 40 kW, and (2) and appurtenant facilities.
A qualifying conduit hydropower facility is one that is determined or deemed to meet all the criteria shown in the table below.

FPA 30(a)(3)(A)
The conduit the facility uses is a tunnel, canal, pipeline, aqueduct, flume, ditch, or similar manmade water conveyance that is operated for the distribution of water for agricultural, municipal, or industrial consumption and not primarily for the generation of electricity
Y
FPA 30(a)(3)(C)(i)
The facility is constructed, operated, or maintained for the generation of electric power and uses for such generation only the hydroelectric potential of a non-federally owned conduit
Y

The proposed Arvin Edison Canal Hydrokinetic 1 Project will not alter the primary purpose of the conduit, which is for agricultural consumption. articles.full_text: This notice announces the appointment of members of the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Senior Executive Service (SES) Performance Review Boards (PRBs) for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The purpose of the PRBs is to make recommendations to the appointing authority (i.e., Agency Head) on the performance of senior executives (career and limited term appointees), including recommendations on performance ratings, performance-based pay adjustments, and performance awards. The PRBs will also make recommendations on the performance of Transportation Security Executive Service, Senior-Level, and Scientific and Professional employees. To make its recommendations, the PRBs will review performance appraisals, initial summary ratings, any response by the employee, and any higher-level official's recommendation.

On March 31, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Peter Michael Wills, D.D.S., of Middletown, Ohio (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 2, at 1, 3. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. AW4788343, alleging that Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Ohio, the state in which [he is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)).[1]
The OSC notified Registrant of his right to file a written request for hearing, and that if he failed to file such a request, he would be deemed to have waived his right to a hearing and be in default.
Id.
at 2 (citing 21 CFR 1301.43). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds him to be in default. RFAA, at 2.[2]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].” 21 CFR 1301.43(e).
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to 21 CFR 1301.43(c), (f), and 1301.46. RFAA, at 3;
see also21 CFR 1316.67.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. According to the OSC, Registrant's Ohio dental license expired by its own terms on December 31, 2025. RFAAX 2, at 1. According to Ohio online records, of which the Agency takes official notice, Registrant's Ohio dental license is expired.[3]
eLicense Ohio Professional Licensure License Lookup,
https://elicense.ohio./oh_verifylicense
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice dentistry in Ohio, the state in which he is registered with DEA.[4]
Discussion
Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3), the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under 21 U.S.C. 823 “upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in
( printed page 66362)
which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. 802(21).”).[5]
The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Craig Cohen, DPM,91 FR 57922 (2026);
Thomas Earley, D.D.S.,91 FR 55624 (2026);
Henry-Norbert O. Ndekwe, M.D.,90 FR 15990 (2025).
According to Ohio statute, “[n]o person shall knowingly obtain, possess, or use a controlled substance or a controlled substance analog,” except pursuant to a “prescription issued by a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs if the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose.” Ohio Rev. Code § 2925.11(A), (B)(1)(d) (2025). Further, a “`[l]icensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs' or `prescriber' means an individual who is authorized by law to prescribe drugs or dangerous drugs or drug therapy related devices in the course of the individual's professional practice.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I). The Ohio statute further defines an authorized prescriber as “[a] dentist licensed under Chapter 4715. of the Revised Code.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I)(1). Additionally, Ohio law permits “[a] licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs, if acting in the course of professional practice, in accordance with the laws regulating the professional's practice” to prescribe or administer schedule II, III, IV, and V controlled substances to patients.
Id.
§ 3719.06(A)(1)(a)-(b).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to practice dentistry in Ohio. As discussed above, an individual must be a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in order to handle controlled substances in Ohio. Thus, because Registrant is not a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in Ohio, and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Ohio, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 824(a), I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. AW4788343 issued to Peter Michael Wills, D.D.S. Further, pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1), I hereby deny any pending applications of Peter Michael Wills, D.D.S., to renew or modify this registration, as well as any other pending application of Peter Michael Wills, D.D.S., for additional registration in Ohio. This Order is effective November 19, 2026.

On March 31, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Jefferson Burroughs, M.D., of Cincinnati, Ohio (Registrant). Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA), Exhibit (RFAAX) 2, at 1, 3. The OSC proposed the revocation of Registrant's Certificate of Registration No. BB2526741, alleging that Registrant is “currently without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Ohio, the state in which [he is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)).[1]
The OSC notified Registrant of his right to file a written request for hearing, and that if he failed to file such a request, he would be deemed to have waived his right to a hearing and be in default.
Id.
at 2 (citing 21 CFR 1301.43). Here, Registrant did not request a hearing, and the Agency finds him to be in default. RFAA, at 2.[2]
“A default, unless excused, shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's/applicant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC].” 21 CFR 1301.43(e).
Further, “[i]n the event that a registrant . . . is deemed to be in default . . . DEA may then file a request for final agency action with the Administrator, along with a record to support its request. In such circumstances, the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to [21 CFR] 1316.67.”
Id.
1301.43(f)(1). Here, the Government has requested final agency action based on Registrant's default pursuant to 21 CFR 1301.43(c), (f), and 1301.46. RFAA, at 3;
see also21 CFR 1316.67.
Findings of Fact
The Agency finds that, in light of Registrant's default, the factual allegations in the OSC are deemed admitted. 21 CFR 1301.43(e).
According to the OSC, on July 1, 2025, Registrant's Ohio medical license expired by its own terms. RFAAX 2, at 1. According to Ohio online records, of which the Agency takes official notice, Registrant's Ohio medical license is expired.[3]
eLicense Ohio Professional Licensure License Lookup,
https://elicense.ohio./oh_verifylicense
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Registrant is not licensed to practice medicine in Ohio, the state in which he is registered with DEA.[4]
Discussion
Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3), the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under 21 U.S.C. 823 “upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.”
With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. 802(21).”).[5]
The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g., Craig Cohen, DPM,91 FR 57922 (2026
); Thomas Earley, D.D.S.,91 FR 55624 (2026);
Henry-Norbert O. Ndekwe, M.D.,90 FR 15990 (2025).
According to Ohio statute, “[n]o person shall knowingly obtain, possess, or use a controlled substance or a controlled substance analog,” except pursuant to a “prescription issued by a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs if the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose.” Ohio Rev. Code §§ 2925.11(A), (B)(1)(d) (2025). Further, a “`[l]icensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs' or `prescriber' means an individual who is authorized by law to prescribe drugs or dangerous drugs or drug therapy related devices in the course of the individual's professional practice.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I) (2026).[6]
The Ohio statute further defines an authorized prescriber as “[a] physician authorized under Chapter 4731. of the Revised Code to practice medicine and surgery, osteopathic medicine and surgery, or podiatric medicine and surgery.”
Id.
§ 4729.01(I)(5) (2026). Additionally, Ohio law permits “[a] licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs, if acting in the course of
( printed page 66361)
professional practice, in accordance with the laws regulating the professional's practice” to prescribe or administer schedule II, III, IV, and V controlled substances to patients.
Id.
§ 3719.06(A)(1)(a)-(b) (2025).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant lacks authority to practice medicine in Ohio. As discussed above, an individual must be a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in order to handle controlled substances in Ohio. Thus, because Registrant is not a licensed health professional authorized to prescribe drugs in Ohio, and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Ohio, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.

I. Background

III. Procedural Requirements
